title: Vital signs and normal adult ranges
note: The classic vital signs are temperature, pulse, respiratory rate and blood pressure, often joined by oxygen saturation. The ranges here are typical values for resting adults from MedlinePlus; reference ranges vary by source, age, fitness and measuring method, so treat them as guides, not sharp cutoffs.

read.title: Taking a blood pressure
text: The classic way to measure blood pressure uses a cuff, a gauge and a stethoscope. The cuff is wrapped around the upper arm at heart level and inflated until it squeezes the brachial artery shut. The examiner then lets the air out slowly while listening over the artery below the cuff.

At first there is silence, because no blood gets through. When cuff pressure drops just below the peak pressure in the artery, blood spurts through with each beat and tapping sounds appear. These are Korotkoff sounds, and the pressure at the first one is the systolic pressure. As the cuff keeps deflating, the sounds change and then vanish when blood flows smoothly again; that point is the diastolic pressure. A reading of 120/80 means a systolic of 120 and a diastolic of 80 millimeters of mercury.

Technique matters. A cuff that is too small for the arm tends to read falsely high, and so can talking or an unsupported arm. Readings also vary through the day, which is why a single high value is rechecked rather than taken as the final word.
